PAPER: Journal of Academic Ethics (2026) 24:36 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09710-3 Review Findings from Ethical Reviews of Non-Medical Research in Japan Takuya Watanabe1 Received: 28 June 2025 / Accepted: 19 November 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract This study examined how ethical reviews are actually conducted in non-medical research in Japan through an analysis of 70 review comments on 19 proposals reviewed by the ethics committee of University A in 2015, using the qualitative method SCAT (Steps for Coding and Theorization). Although non-medical research generally lacks the physical invasiveness characteristic of medical research, appropriate ethical considerations remain essential. The comments were classified into seven categories, with “Scientific rational- ity of the research plan,” “Request for cooperation,” and “Assessment of risks and ben- efits” being the most frequent. To facilitate interpretation, these categories were further organized into four overarching themes: (1) Methodological commitment, (2) Participant selection and protection, (3) Research benefits and foreseeable risks, and (4) Researcher’s inadequate ethical reflections. Reviewers often required clearer articulation of research objectives, background, and methods, as well as more detailed explanations and consent procedures for participants, including attention to minors and withdrawal rights. These findings suggest that ethical review in non-medical research should go beyond procedural formality to ensure careful consideration of research purpose, participant rights, and po- tential risks, thereby supporting ethically sound research practices. Keywords Ethical review · Review findings · Research ethics committee · Non-medical research Introduction In non-medical research, typified by studies in the humanities and social sciences, there is no intention to intervene through medical acts such as diagnosis or treatment of specific diseases, and compared to medical research, the physical invasiveness posed to participants is generally minimal. Previous discussions have raised concerns about treating non-medical Takuya Watanabe t.watanabe82@gmail.com 1 Department of Ethics Support, Kyoto University Hospital, 53, Shogoin Kawahara-cho, Sakyo- ku, Kyoto 606-8507, Japan 1 3 36 Page 2 of 11 T. Watanabe research in the same way as medical research (i.e., applying the same research regulations), and there have been negative opinions regarding this approach (Colnerud, 2015; Grady, 2010; Wynn, 2018). Nevertheless, several scholars argue that these concerns may be over- stated, suggesting that non-medical research may not always require less stringent ethi- cal review (Hansson, 2020; Hunter, 2014). Non-medical research may involve significant potential risks, including emotional stress, breaches of privacy, and stigmatization. At the same time, little is known about the extent of protection required by research participants (Sauerland et al., 2019). Therefore, adhering strictly to the same regulations as medical research is not necessarily appropriate, and ethical considerations tailored to the specific nature of non-medical research are deemed necessary. At the same time, there are aspects where medical and non-medical research overlap. Although non-medical research rarely involves physical invasiveness, some types of medical research—such as register-based or retrospective observational studies—also involve minimal or no physical intervention. In this respect, medical and non-medical research share similarities, particularly in how they handle personal data. In Japan, there is no unified regulation, such as government-imposed research rules, for non-medical research. It has been reported that ethics committees reviewing such stud- ies have conducted ethical reviews based on various operational standards. For example, the operational standards and review systems of ethics committees vary by university, and the perspectives emphasized during ethical reviews—particularly in regard to the scien- tific rationality of research plans—also vary, suggesting that certain innovations have been implemented (Ujihara, 2023; Watanabe et al., 2022). Outside Japan, there have been proposals regarding the systems and functions of ethical review in non-medical research (Bülow et al., 2024; Lindorff, 2010; Van Heerden et al., 2016). Although these studies suggest the institutional direction of ethical review, they lack reference to the concrete content of the reviews and are inadequate for grasping the current realities and challenges of ethical review in non-medical research. While investigations into the operational standards and review structures of ethics committees or recommendations on the system and function of ethical review can provide an outline of ethical review, they do not offer insight into the substantive aspects—namely, the actual content of the reviews. Thus, such information is inadequate for understanding how ethical review is truly con- ducted in non-medical research. To closely grasp the realities of ethical review, it is considered useful to examine the actual review comments issued by university ethics committees, as well as the perspectives of these committees (i.e., the stance of reviewers during ethical deliberations) (Ohnishi et al., 2021; Suzuki & Sato, 2010). However, at present, such efforts regarding ethical review in non-medical research are rarely seen in Japan. In contrast, for medical research, the cur- rent “Ethical Guidelines for Life Science and Medical Research Involving Human Subjects” stipulate that “the organization establishing the ethics review committee must publish, at least once a year, the status of committee meetings and a summary of reviews via the ‘Eth- ics Review Committee Reporting System’ under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare” (Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology et al., 2021). Through this system, it is possible to obtain information related to review content and grasp the actual state of ethical review. Ethics committees or their administrative offices can refer to this information and apply it to practice. For the committee in question, it can serve as material for self-inspection and evaluation to reflect on the quality of their reviews; 1 3 Review Findings from Ethical Reviews of Non-Medical Research in Japan Page 3 of 11 36 for other committees, it can be used as a reference to compare their own review practices with those of other institutions. However, in the case of non-medical research, no government-imposed research regula- tion has been established to date in Japan, and information regarding the content of reviews is rarely made public. As a result, it is extremely difficult for third parties to grasp the details of specific ethics committees’ review content (Watanabe, 2018). In some countries, ethical review of social science and humanities research has already been a well-established practice (Schrag, 2011). Recently, ethical review systems have been further expanding to cover an even wider range of non-medical research (Carniel et al., 2022; Davies, 2020; Hansson, 2020). Even so, studies that have examined ethics commit- tees reviewing non-medical research remain limited, and further development of knowledge and perspectives regarding the appropriate nature of ethical review is still needed. In such a context, for ethics committees to avoid ad hoc reviews, it is necessary to examine the practical and essential elements of ethical review. In addition, there is a lack of accessible reference information to facilitate such examination. Therefore, this study aims to concretely understand the actual practices of ethical review in non-medical research by closely analyzing the review comments issued by one univer- sity’s ethics committee, which cooperated with the study. The ethics committee of Univer- sity A conducts a preliminary review through face-to-face meetings between reviewers and applicants, allowing procedural and ethical issues to be discussed and clarified before the formal review process. By examining these review comments, the study seeks to grasp the perspectives of the ethics committee–specifically, how those perspectives are reflected in the content of the reviews–at a practical level. To clearly define “non-medical research,” this study treated as non-medical any research that did not fall under the definition of medi- cal research as outlined in the “Ethical Guidelines for Life Science and Medical Research Involving Human Subjects.” Specifically, the guidelines define medical research as studies aimed at (1) acquiring knowledge that contributes to the maintenance and promotion of public health or the recovery of patients from disease or the improvement of their quality of life through understanding the causes and pathology of diseases, improving or validat- ing prevention methods, and verifying or improving the effectiveness of diagnostic and therapeutic methods in medical practice; and (2) acquiring knowledge about the structure or function of the human genome and genes, or genetic mutations or expressions, using human-derived specimens or information. Research involving human subjects not falling into either of these categories was considered non-medical in this study. Methods This study analyzed the review comments for all 19 non-medical research proposals newly reviewed in 2015 by the ethics committee of University A in Japan. The ethics committee of University A states that it reviews studies involving human subjects that do not fall under the category of medical research as defined in the aforementioned guidelines. Among the 19 research proposals, 13 were submitted by graduate students, 3 by research fellows, and 3 by faculty members. The reviewed proposals covered various academic fields, including psychology (n = 12), sociology (n = 5), art studies (n = 1), and linguistics (n = 1). Key ethical issues are primarily addressed during the preliminary review stage. Therefore, all 70 review comments issued during the preliminary reviews were selected for analysis. All 19 proposals received approval in the final review stage. To analyze the 70 review comments, this study employed SCAT (Steps for Coding and Theorization), a method proposed by Otani (2008, 2011). SCAT is considered effective for analyzing small-scale text data and enables simple and transparent coding and categoriza- tion of textual content. In this study, each of the 70 review comments was analyzed accord- ing to the SCAT procedure, which involved the following steps: 1. Keyword extraction: Identifying important terms and phrases within the review comments 2. Paraphrasing and supplementing related concepts: Rephrasing the content from Step 1 and adding related concepts. 3. Describing underlying meanings and implications: Interpreting the context, intention, and background behind the content from Step 2. 4. Categorization: Integrating the concepts derived in Step 3 into broader thematic categories. Example: 1. Keyword extraction: “Informed consent,” “adequate explanation” 2. Paraphrasing and supplementing related concepts: “The procedure for obtaining con- sent was insufficient,” “It is necessary to provide information that research participants can understand” 3. Describing underlying meanings and implications: Emphasis is placed on the research- er’s responsibility to explain when recruiting participants, as well as the importance of respecting the autonomy of participants and the will of their proxies 4. Categorization: “Request for cooperation” To ensure the trustworthiness of the SCAT analysis process, the coding steps were cross- checked by the author and a research assistant with experience in qualitative research—who was a third party not involved in the relevant ethics committee. The inter-coder agreement rate between the author and the research assistant was κ =.81, indicating that the categoriza- tion was reliably conducted. 1 3 Review Findings from Ethical Reviews of Non-Medical Research in Japan Page 5 of 11 36 Table 2 Classification of review Category; Example comments No. of comments comments Scientific rationality of the research plan 21 Clarify what the study aims to elucidate. Results As a result of the SCAT analysis, the review comments were classified into seven categories (Table 2). To facilitate interpretation, these categories were further organized into four overarch- ing themes: (1) Methodological commitment, (2) Participant selection and protection, (3) Research benefits and foreseeable risks, and (4) Researcher’s inadequate ethical reflections. 1 3 36 Page 6 of 11 T. Watanabe Methodological Commitment The most frequently occurring category was “Scientific rationality of the research plan,” accounting for 30% (21 comments) of all review comments. Examples included remarks related to the significance of the research, such as “Clarify what the study aims to elucidate” and “Explain the purpose and significance of the study based on its background.” Addition- ally, regarding research procedures, comments included “Describe in detail what will be observed,” “Describe the visual stimuli in detail,” “Provide an outline of the tests to be conducted,” “If the methods are based on prior studies, clearly indicate this,” and “Explain the usefulness of examining test-retest reliability.” These comments pointed out a lack of clarity in the research’s purpose, background, and methods. When insufficient explanation was found regarding the research’s purpose and significance, additional clarification was requested. Moreover, the ethics committee went further into the specifics of each research plan, checking detailed descriptions of methods such as surveys, experiments, observations, and interviews, as well as the utility of those methods. Participant Selection and Protection Following “Scientific rationality of the research plan,” the next most frequent category was “Request for cooperation,” accounting for 27% (19 comments). Examples included remarks such as “Clearly specify in the explanatory document the research purpose and significance, personal information protection, material handling, and consent withdrawal procedures” and “If minors are included, consider obtaining parental consent.” Reviewers frequently pointed out insufficient detail in explanatory documents for recruiting participants, lack of procedures for obtaining substitute consent when involving minors, and inadequate ethical consideration for those surrounding the participants. The comments also highlighted the need for sufficient explanation regarding the research content, methods of disseminating results, and handling of personal and research data. Furthermore, to ensure the protection of participants’ rights (particularly autonomy), several review comments were issued when there was insufficient (or overly simplified) explanation that participants would not suffer disadvantages if they refused to cooperate or later withdrew their consent. The categories “Fairness in participant selection” (11%, 8 comments) and “Privacy pro- tection” (3%, 2 comments) were also included in this theme, addressing issues such as the appropriateness of participant selection and the anonymization of personal information. Examples included remarks such as “Clarify the appropriateness of participant selection” for “Fairness in participant selection,” and “Manage personal information in anonymized form” for “Privacy protection.” Research Benefits and Foreseeable Risks In this theme, which included the category “Assessment of risks and benefits” (14%, 10 comments), reviewers emphasized the need to justify claims that research would not involve any burden or risk. Comments included: “Indicate the degree of burden associated with the questionnaire,” “Clarify the rationale for ensuring that no harm will come to participants,” and “Consider measures to address participant fatigue.” These findings confirm that the 1 3 Review Findings from Ethical Reviews of Non-Medical Research in Japan Page 7 of 11 36 burdens and risks associated with non-medical research are central points in ethical review deliberations. This theme also encompassed “Confirmation regarding remuneration” (3%, 2 com- ments), where reviewers examined whether compensation would be offered and how it would be presented, as part of the overall evaluation of participant benefit and fairness. Examples included remarks such as “Clearly state the method of providing remuneration” related to “Confirmation regarding remuneration.” Researcher’s Inadequate Ethical Reflections The category “Management of personal information and research data” (11%, 8 comments) was grouped under this theme. Examples included remarks such as “Clarify plans for data storage and disposal.” Comments in this category addressed issues such as methods and periods of data storage, as well as insufficient researcher awareness regarding the ethical implications of data handling. These comments suggest that the ethics committee placed emphasis not only on procedural compliance but also on the researcher’s ethical self-reflec- tion in planning and conducting research. Discussion To maintain consistency with the Results section, this discussion refers to the four overarch- ing themes identified in the analysis: “Methodological commitment,” “Participant selection and protection,” “Research benefits and foreseeable risks,” and “Researcher’s inadequate ethical reflections.” Although seven categories were identified through SCAT analysis, this discussion focuses primarily on the three most frequently observed themes—“Methodological com- mitment,” “Participant selection and protection,” and “Research benefits and foreseeable risks.” These three themes accounted for over 70% of all review comments and most clearly reflect the core concerns raised by the ethics committee. The first theme, “Methodological commitment” (which included comments categorized as “Scientific rationality of the research plan”), was the most frequently observed. One pos- sible reason for this is that the preliminary review serves as a primary screening process. At this stage—prior to the formal review by the ethics committee—information is organized to grasp the overall structure of the research plan. Therefore, if the overall research plan is unclear or individual elements are insufficiently described, these points are more likely to be highlighted in the review. Among the most frequently raised concerns were inadequate explanations of the research’s purpose and significance. There was also a tendency to delve into the methodological aspects, requesting detailed descriptions of the procedures and jus- tifications for the chosen methods. When such information is included, it enables a more comprehensive understanding of the research plan, which is essential for a thorough ethical review. In other words, the contents of the research proposal serve as vital information for anticipating potential ethical issues. However, the frequent comments in this category sug- gest that this awareness may not yet be fully shared among researchers. Another possible interpretation is that, in some cases, the ethics committee may impose somewhat excessive 1 3 36 Page 8 of 11 T. Watanabe requirements on researchers, requesting highly detailed descriptions in the research plan— including aspects that may be difficult to specify prior to the start of the study. Within the second theme, “Participant selection and protection” (which encompassed comments categorized as “Request for cooperation,” “Fairness in participant selection,” and “Privacy protection”), it was required that information necessary for potential partici- pants (or their representatives) to make an informed decision about cooperation be pre- sented accurately. These comments pointed out deficiencies in explanations of the research procedures, dissemination of results, and handling of personal and research data. However, what stood out most were the concerns related to ensuring the rights of research participants, particularly their autonomy. When applications lacked a clear statement that refusal to par- ticipate or withdrawal of consent would not result in any disadvantage to the participant—or when such statements were overly simplified—those omissions were consistently noted in the review comments. Although these explanations represent a fundamental ethical con- sideration in human research, they pose a dilemma. There is a perceived trade-off between ethical compliance and scientific pursuit (Sugimori et al., 2004). From the researcher’s per- spective, providing such explanations may be seen as potentially hindering the progress of the study by encouraging participants to easily withdraw. As a result, researchers may be tempted to simplify or omit such explanations, but doing so is likely to attract criticism from the ethics committee. The frequency of review comments in this category suggests that the ethics committee adopts a stringent stance, similarly to medical research, grounded in the principle of informed consent—that is, participants should be “fully informed and autono- mously consenting.” The third theme, “Research benefits and foreseeable risks” (which included comments categorized as “Assessment of risks and benefits” and “Confirmation regarding remu- neration”), reflects the specific characteristics of ethical review in non-medical research. Compared to medical research, non-medical studies typically involve minimal physical invasiveness. However, the possibility of psychological harm to participants, or violations of their rights and welfare, cannot be entirely ruled out. These risks are often overlooked, but for example, in surveys or interviews dealing with highly sensitive topics, the act of responding itself may impose psychological burdens on participants. Furthermore, the dis- closure of research findings could lead to prejudice or discrimination against participants, which constitutes a social risk that cannot be dismissed. If researchers underestimate the burdens or risks associated with their studies, they may also overlook essential ethical considerations, leading to inadequate protection for participants. Review comments were consistently issued whenever the application stated that there were “no burdens or risks” to participants. This demonstrates the ethics committee’s important role in encouraging researchers to critically reflect on the burdens and risks associated with their studies. It can thus be said that providing researchers with an opportunity to engage seriously with the ethical dimensions of their research is a key function of ethics committees reviewing non-medical research. At the same time, it is difficult to apply uniform interpretations to the assessment of burdens and risks or to the notion of benefits. These judgments may be implicitly influenced by cultural values and social norms. Therefore, it is important to take such possibilities into account when considering the background of the review comments. Finally, the fourth theme—“Researcher’s inadequate ethical reflections” (which included comments categorized as “Management of personal information and research data”)—cap- tured comments emphasizing researchers’ insufficient awareness of ethical implications, 1 3 Review Findings from Ethical Reviews of Non-Medical Research in Japan Page 9 of 11 36 such as the management of personal information and research data. This theme highlights that the ethics committee’s expectations extend beyond procedural compliance to include researchers’ ethical self-reflection in planning and conducting research. It suggests that ethi- cal review in non-medical contexts plays an educational role, prompting researchers to criti- cally engage with the ethical dimensions of their practices rather than treating the review merely as an administrative requirement. Ethical issues manifest in various ways depending on the diversity of research practices (e.g., surveys, experiments, observations, interviews), participants (ranging from infants to the elderly, from healthy individuals to patients and persons with disabilities), and research settings (from laboratory experiments to field studies in clinical environments such as healthcare and welfare institutions). These variations make it difficult to apply uniform ethi- cal standards across non-medical research. In this regard, the Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct of the Ameri- can Psychological Association includes a provision that allows for the waiver of informed consent in certain types of research where no harm or discomfort is anticipated and par- ticipant confidentiality is ensured (American Psychological Association, 2017). Under the “Research and Publication” section, the clause titled “Dispensing with Informed Consent for Research” provides an example of a context-sensitive approach to ethical review. In contrast, within the scope of this study, the ethics committee consistently required revi- sions whenever explanatory documents for participant recruitment were found insufficient, regardless of the nature of the study. This suggests that Japanese ethics committees tend to adopt a more cautious and uniform stance toward informed consent, even in low-risk non- medical research, possibly reflecting institutional or cultural orientations toward participant protection. Limitations In order to understand the actual practice of ethical review in non-medical research at a practical level, this study closely examined the content of review comments that were actu- ally issued. Permission was granted to review only one year’s worth of review comments, and only for research projects that had already been completed. Although the analysis was limited to review comments from preliminary reviews conducted by a single ethics commit- tee and covered only a one-year period, it was considered to provide sufficient qualitative information. Therefore, this study offers useful insights for understanding the actual prac- tices of ethical review in non-medical research from a practical perspective. At the same time, there are some limitations: it was not possible to examine how researchers responded to the review comments, and the analysis focused solely on the preliminary reviews of a single ethics committee. Accordingly, while the findings of this study may be applicable to similar contexts, they cannot necessarily be taken to represent the general state of ethical review in non-medical research. Therefore, the findings of this study cannot be taken to represent the general state of ethical review in non-medical research. Nevertheless, given the current lack of publicly available information on the actual practices of ethical review in non-medical research, the findings of this study may offer useful insights for understanding how such reviews are conducted. 1 3 36 Page 10 of 11 T. Watanabe Conclusion This study analyzed the actual review comments from a university ethics committee to clarify how ethical reviews are conducted in non-medical research. The findings indicated that ethical review in this context places particular emphasis on the scientific rationality of the research plan and the protection of participants’ rights and welfare. These results highlight that ethical review in non-medical research should not be a mere procedural formality but a process that encourages researchers to reflect on the ethical dimensions of their work and ensures that participant rights are safeguarded throughout the research process. JSON: Name: nonmedical_ethics_review_pipeline Title: SCAT-guided mixed-methods and supervised classification pipeline to characterize and generalize ethics committee review themes for non-medical research in Japan Short Hypothesis: A supervised classifier trained on SCAT-coded ethics committee review comments from one Japanese university will predict the four overarching themes in review comments from other Japanese universities with macro-F1 ≥ 0.80. Related Work: Existing approaches to studying ethics committee review practices fall into two classes: manual qualitative coding (small-sample methods such as SCAT, grounded theory, and thematic analysis) and institutional reporting systems (aggregated, often quantitative summaries). Manual qualitative methods provide high interpretive fidelity but are limited by small samples, single-institution scope, low reproducibility, and heavy annotator labor. Institutional reporting systems provide scale but lack content granularity and cross-institution comparability. Prior comparative studies document variability in operational standards across committees but do not analyze the textual content of review comments at scale. There is no established public labeled corpus of ethics review comments for non-medical research, and automated classification of review-comment themes has not been systematically evaluated. Thus current methods either sacrifice depth for scale or depth for breadth and leave open the problems of cross-institution generalization, reproducible coding protocols, and automated scaling. Abstract: Understanding how ethics committees evaluate non-medical research requires reproducible analysis of review content and scalable methods to generalize across institutions. We propose a mixed-methods research pipeline that combines SCAT-based manual coding of review comments with supervised natural language classification to map and validate recurring review themes. The pipeline defines a coding schema anchored in four overarching themes (methodological commitment, participant selection and protection, research benefits and risks, researcher ethical reflection), produces a vetted labeled dataset, trains and evaluates multiple classifiers under cross-institution transfer conditions, and provides quantitative reports and qualitative exemplars. The main contributions are (1) an explicit SCAT-derived coding protocol for ethics review comments, (2) a labeled dataset and inter-annotator reliability procedures, (3) a supervised classification benchmark including cross-institution generalization and ablation studies, and (4) analysis outputs that identify systematic emphases and gaps in ethics review practice. Expected outcomes include a reproducible toolset for scaling content-level study of ethics reviews and empirical evidence on theme generalizability across Japanese institutions. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Seed dataset: 70 SCAT-coded review comments from University A (2015) with labels at comment level mapping to 7 SCAT categories and 4 overarching themes. (2) Expansion dataset: collect de-identified review comments from 10 additional Japanese universities, target n=1,500 total comments (approx. 150 per university) covering multiple years and disciplines. Annotation: dual independent coders per comment using the SCAT-derived schema, adjudication, report Cohen's kappa. Train/Validation/Test splits: stratified by theme and institution: 70% train, 10% validation, 20% test. Cross-institution evaluation: leave-one-university-out (LOUO) tests; also hold-out a wholly unseen university for final generalization. Baselines: (A) majority-class baseline, (B) rule-based keyword classifier using SCAT lexicon, (C) TF-IDF + logistic regression, (D) linear SVM, (E) fine-tuned Japanese BERT (or language-appropriate transformer) classifier. Metrics: per-class precision, recall, F1; macro-F1; micro-F1; accuracy; inter-annotator Cohen's kappa for human labels. Experimental setup: train each model on pooled training data, validate hyperparameters on validation set, evaluate on test and on each LOUO hold-out. Ablation studies: (1) remove SCAT preprocessing and train on raw labels to measure impact of SCAT-derived features, (2) train with progressively smaller labeled sets (100%, 50%, 25% of training data) to measure label-efficiency, (3) ablate lexical features from the best model to measure dependence on keywords. Error analysis: confusion matrices, qualitative sampling of false positives/negatives per theme. Reporting: all splits, seeds, hyperparameters, and evaluation code made reproducible; report statistical significance of model differences using paired bootstrap tests. Risk Factors and Limitations: Limited availability and access restrictions to ethics review comments due to confidentiality and institutional policies will constrain dataset size and sampling diversity. De-identification may remove context necessary for accurate coding, introducing annotation noise. Annotation bias and low inter-annotator agreement for nuanced categories are possible, particularly across disciplines. Class imbalance among themes (e.g., methodological comments dominating) may inflate some metrics and hinder minority-theme performance. Cross-institution variability in terminology, document format, and review procedures may limit classifier transferability and reduce generalization beyond sampled institutions. Cultural and language-specific constructs may prevent direct application of models to non-Japanese contexts. Small initial seed datasets (e.g., 70 comments) limit pretraining utility and risk model overfitting to seed-specific patterns. Legal and ethical constraints may prevent sharing raw data, reducing reproducibility of downstream researchers. Computational limitations may arise for transformer fine-tuning on Japanese legal/ethical text if domain-adaptive pretraining is required but resources are insufficient.
